entry.sum: Many quantities (area, volume, length, work, total change) are built by cutting an object into thin pieces, approximating each piece by something simple, and adding: in the limit the sum becomes an integral. The one idea to remember is the recipe 'slice, approximate, sum, take the limit', for example $V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx$ where $A(x)$ is the area of the cross-section at $x$.
entry.why: These formulas are how calculus is actually used: the volume of a tank, the work needed to pump it empty, the distance travelled from a speedometer record, and the average temperature over a day are all integrals of this kind.

links.note: Volumes of solids such as cones, balls and tori, and Cavalieri's principle, follow from integrating areas of cross-sections.
Probabilities and expected values of continuous random variables are areas and weighted averages computed as integrals of a density.

refs: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals
Apostol, Calculus, Vol. 1
Spivak, Calculus

blocks.body:
A car's speedometer is recorded every second. How far did the car go? A vase has a curved profile. How much water does it hold? A spring gets harder to stretch the further you pull it. How much effort does stretching it take? None of these is a simple 'rate times time' or 'length times width' calculation, because the quantity being multiplied keeps changing.

The [[ftc|fundamental theorem of calculus]] tells us how to evaluate integrals; this page is about recognising when a quantity is an integral and setting the integral up correctly. The same four-step recipe works every time: slice, approximate each slice, add, and let the slices get thin.

blocks.title: The recipe: slice, approximate, sum, limit
blocks.body:
Suppose a quantity $Q$ is spread along an interval $[a,b]$, and on a short piece $[x, x+\Delta x]$ it is approximately $q(x)\,\Delta x$ for some function $q$. Cut $[a,b]$ into $n$ pieces of width $\Delta x = (b-a)/n$ with sample points $x_1, \dots, x_n$. Then

$$Q \approx \sum_{i=1}^{n} q(x_i)\,\Delta x.$$

This is a Riemann sum (see [[riemann-integral]]). The error in each slice is small compared with $\Delta x$ itself, so as $n \to \infty$ the total error goes to $0$ and $Q = \int_a^b q(x)\,dx$.

Here is the recipe in action on a quantity whose answer we already know. Water flows into a tank at rate $r(t) = 2t$ litres per minute. In the first minute the rate rises from 0 to 2; with 4 slices of a quarter-minute, using the rate at the left end of each slice, the estimate is $\tfrac14(0 + 0.5 + 1 + 1.5) = 0.75$ litres; using right ends it is $\tfrac14(0.5+1+1.5+2) = 1.25$. With 100 slices the two estimates are $0.99$ and $1.01$. They squeeze in on $\int_0^1 2t\,dt = 1$.

The real skill is the middle step: deciding what a thin slice looks like and what simple shape approximates it. Once you have written $q(x)\,\Delta x$, the integral follows.

blocks.title: Area between curves
blocks.body:
If $f(x) \ge g(x)$ on $[a,b]$, a thin vertical strip at $x$ is nearly a rectangle of height $f(x) - g(x)$ and width $\Delta x$. So the area of the region between the graphs is

$$A = \int_a^b \bigl(f(x) - g(x)\bigr)\,dx.$$

Example: between $y = x$ and $y = x^2$ on $[0,1]$ the line is on top, and $A = \int_0^1 (x - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac12 - \tfrac13 = \tfrac16$.

Two practical points. First, the limits $a$, $b$ are usually where the curves cross, found by solving $f(x) = g(x)$. Second, if the curves swap places, split the interval: the area is $\int_a^b |f - g|\,dx$, not $\int_a^b (f-g)\,dx$. Sometimes horizontal strips are easier: if the region is bounded on the left by $x = p(y)$ and on the right by $x = q(y)$, then $A = \int_c^d (q(y) - p(y))\,dy$.

blocks.title: Net change, motion and average value
blocks.body:
If $F' = f$, the fundamental theorem says $\int_a^b f(t)\,dt = F(b) - F(a)$: integrating a rate gives the total change. Physically, if $v(t)$ is the velocity of a particle moving on a line, then $\int_a^b v(t)\,dt$ is its displacement $x(b) - x(a)$. Time spent moving backwards counts negatively. The distance travelled is $\int_a^b |v(t)|\,dt$, which is larger whenever the particle reverses.

The same idea gives accumulation functions. A tank holds 50 litres at time $0$; water enters at 6 litres per minute and leaks out at $2t$ litres per minute. The volume at time $t$ is $V(t) = 50 + \int_0^t (6 - 2s)\,ds = 50 + 6t - t^2$. It is largest when the net rate $6 - 2t$ is zero, at $t = 3$, where $V = 59$ litres.

The average value of $f$ on $[a,b]$ is defined by

$$\bar f = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

It is the limit of ordinary averages of $f(x_1), \dots, f(x_n)$ at equally spaced points, since $\frac1n\sum f(x_i) = \frac{1}{b-a}\sum f(x_i)\Delta x$. Geometrically, $\bar f$ is the height of the rectangle on $[a,b]$ with the same area as the region under the graph. For $f(x) = x^2$ on $[0,3]$, $\bar f = \tfrac13 \cdot 9 = 3$.

blocks.title: Mean value theorem for integrals
blocks.body:
If $f$ is continuous on $[a,b]$, there is a point $c \in [a,b]$ with

$$f(c) = \frac{1}{b-a}\int_a^b f(x)\,dx.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: By the extreme value theorem (see [[continuity]]) $f$ has a minimum $m$ and a maximum $M$ on $[a,b]$. Since $m \le f(x) \le M$, integrating gives $m(b-a) \le \int_a^b f \le M(b-a)$, so the average $\bar f$ lies between $m$ and $M$. These values are taken by $f$ at some points of $[a,b]$, so by the intermediate value theorem $f$ takes the value $\bar f$ at some $c$ between them. For $x^2$ on $[0,3]$ the point is $c = \sqrt 3$.

blocks.title: Volume by slicing: discs, washers and shells
blocks.body:
Cut a solid by planes perpendicular to the $x$-axis. If the cross-section at $x$ has area $A(x)$, a slice of thickness $\Delta x$ is nearly a flat slab of volume $A(x)\,\Delta x$, so

$$V = \int_a^b A(x)\,dx.$$

A cone of height $h$ and base radius $r$, with apex at the origin and axis along the $x$-axis, has circular cross-sections of radius $rx/h$. So $V = \int_0^h \pi r^2 x^2/h^2\,dx = \tfrac13 \pi r^2 h$, the formula from school geometry. A ball of radius $r$ has cross-sections of radius $\sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$, and $V = \int_{-r}^{r}\pi(r^2 - x^2)\,dx = \tfrac43\pi r^3$. The formula also explains Cavalieri's principle: two solids whose cross-sections at every height have equal areas have equal volumes.

Solids of revolution. Rotating the region under $y = f(x) \ge 0$ about the $x$-axis gives circular cross-sections (discs), $V = \int_a^b \pi f(x)^2\,dx$. If the region lies between $g \le f$, the cross-section is a washer (a disc with a hole) and $V = \int_a^b \pi(f^2 - g^2)\,dx$.

Rotating about the $y$-axis instead, it can be easier to slice the region into thin vertical strips. The strip at distance $x$ from the axis sweeps out a thin cylindrical shell of radius $x$, height $f(x) - g(x)$ and thickness $\Delta x$; unrolled, it is nearly a flat plate of volume $2\pi x\,(f(x) - g(x))\,\Delta x$. Hence the shell formula

$$V = \int_a^b 2\pi x\,\bigl(f(x) - g(x)\bigr)\,dx.$$

Discs and shells are two ways of slicing the same solid, so they must agree. For the region between $y = x^2$ and $y = x$ on $[0,1]$ rotated about the $y$-axis: shells give $2\pi\int_0^1 x(x - x^2)\,dx = 2\pi(\tfrac13 - \tfrac14) = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$; washers, slicing horizontally at height $y$ with outer radius $\sqrt y$ and inner radius $y$, give $\pi\int_0^1 (y - y^2)\,dy = \tfrac{\pi}{6}$.

blocks.title: Arc length
blocks.body:
To measure the length of the graph of a smooth function $f$ on $[a,b]$, replace the curve over $[x, x+\Delta x]$ by its chord. By Pythagoras the chord has length $\sqrt{\Delta x^2 + \Delta y^2} = \sqrt{1 + (\Delta y/\Delta x)^2}\,\Delta x$, and by the [[mvt|mean value theorem]] $\Delta y/\Delta x = f'(\xi)$ for some $\xi$ in the slice. Summing and taking the limit,

$$L = \int_a^b \sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx.$$

The square root means most arc-length integrals have no simple closed form (already for $y = x^2$ a logarithm appears), so examples are chosen to make $1 + f'^2$ a perfect square. For $y = \tfrac23 x^{3/2}$ on $[0,3]$, $f'(x) = \sqrt x$ and $L = \int_0^3 \sqrt{1+x}\,dx = \tfrac23(4^{3/2} - 1) = \tfrac{14}{3}$. For curves given by parameters, see [[parametric-polar]].

blocks.title: Work
blocks.body:
If a constant force $F$ pushes an object a distance $d$ in the direction of the force, the work done is $W = Fd$. If the force varies with position, $F = F(x)$, then over a short step $\Delta x$ it is nearly constant and the work is nearly $F(x)\,\Delta x$, so $W = \int_a^b F(x)\,dx$.

Springs. Hooke's law says that holding a spring stretched $x$ beyond its natural length takes force $kx$. If a force of 10 N holds a spring stretched 0.2 m, then $k = 50$ N/m, and the work to stretch it from 0.2 m to 0.5 m is $\int_{0.2}^{0.5} 50x\,dx = 25(0.25 - 0.04) = 5.25$ J.

Pumping. Here we slice the liquid, not the path: each thin layer is lifted a different distance. A cylindrical tank of radius 1 m and height 3 m is full of water (density $\rho = 1000$ kg/m$^3$, $g = 9.8$ m/s$^2$). The layer at height $y$ above the bottom, of thickness $\Delta y$, has weight $\rho g \pi \cdot 1^2\,\Delta y$ and must be lifted $3 - y$ metres to the top. So

$$W = \int_0^3 \rho g\pi(3 - y)\,dy = \rho g \pi \cdot \tfrac92 = 44100\pi \approx 1.385 \times 10^5 \text{ J}.$$

blocks.title: Area enclosed by a parabola and a line
blocks.body: Find the area of the region enclosed by $y = 4 - x^2$ and $y = x + 2$.
blocks.solution:
The curves meet where $4 - x^2 = x + 2$, that is $x^2 + x - 2 = 0$, so $x = -2$ or $x = 1$. At $x = 0$ the parabola gives 4 and the line gives 2, so the parabola is on top throughout $(-2, 1)$. The area is

$$\int_{-2}^{1}\bigl(4 - x^2 - (x+2)\bigr)\,dx = \Bigl[2x - \tfrac{x^2}{2} - \tfrac{x^3}{3}\Bigr]_{-2}^{1} = \tfrac76 - \bigl(-\tfrac{10}{3}\bigr) = \tfrac92.$$

A check: for a parabola $y = -x^2 + px + q$ and a line meeting it at $x = \alpha$ and $x = \beta$, the difference of the two is $(x-\alpha)(\beta-x)$, whose integral over $[\alpha,\beta]$ is $(\beta-\alpha)^3/6$ (a modern form of Archimedes' quadrature of the parabola). Here $\beta - \alpha = 3$ and $27/6 = 9/2$.

blocks.title: Displacement versus distance
blocks.body: A particle moves on a line with velocity $v(t) = t^2 - 4t + 3$ m/s for $0 \le t \le 4$. Find its displacement and the total distance it travels.
blocks.solution:
An antiderivative is $F(t) = \tfrac{t^3}{3} - 2t^2 + 3t$, so the displacement is $F(4) - F(0) = \tfrac{64}{3} - 32 + 12 = \tfrac43$ m.

For the distance we need to know where $v$ changes sign. Since $v(t) = (t-1)(t-3)$, the particle moves forward on $[0,1]$, backward on $[1,3]$ and forward on $[3,4]$. Now $F(0) = 0$, $F(1) = \tfrac43$, $F(3) = 0$, $F(4) = \tfrac43$, so the three legs have lengths $\tfrac43$, $\tfrac43$ and $\tfrac43$, and the total distance is $4$ m. The displacement is only a third of the distance because the backward leg cancels one forward leg.

blocks.title: Two cylinders crossing
blocks.body: Two solid circular cylinders of radius $r$ have axes that meet at right angles. Find the volume of the solid common to both (the Steinmetz solid). Neither discs nor shells apply directly; find a good direction to slice.
blocks.solution:
Put the axes along the $x$-axis and the $y$-axis, so the cylinders are $y^2 + z^2 \le r^2$ and $x^2 + z^2 \le r^2$. Slice by horizontal planes $z = $ constant. In such a plane the first cylinder gives $|y| \le \sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$ and the second gives $|x| \le \sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$, so the cross-section is a square of side $2\sqrt{r^2 - z^2}$ and area $4(r^2 - z^2)$. Therefore

$$V = \int_{-r}^{r} 4(r^2 - z^2)\,dz = 4\Bigl(2r^3 - \tfrac{2r^3}{3}\Bigr) = \tfrac{16}{3}r^3.$$

There is a pretty comparison. The ball of radius $r$ centred at the origin sits inside this solid, and its cross-section at height $z$ is the disc inscribed in the square. The ratio of disc to square is $\pi/4$ at every height, so by Cavalieri's principle the ball has $\pi/4$ of the volume: $\tfrac{\pi}{4}\cdot\tfrac{16}{3}r^3 = \tfrac43\pi r^3$. Archimedes knew this result without calculus.

blocks.title: Beyond the basic formulas
blocks.body:
Centres of mass: a thin plate occupying the region under $y = f(x)$, with uniform density, balances at $\bar x = \frac{1}{A}\int_a^b x f(x)\,dx$, the average of $x$ weighted by strip area. Combining this with the shell formula gives Pappus's centroid theorem: rotating a plane region of area $A$ about an axis it does not cross produces a solid of volume $2\pi \bar r A$, where $\bar r$ is the distance from the axis to the centroid. Indeed, the shell formula is $\int 2\pi x\,h(x)\,dx = 2\pi \cdot \bigl(\frac1A\int x\,h(x)\,dx\bigr)\cdot A$. A torus, obtained by rotating a disc of radius $a$ whose centre is at distance $R > a$ from the axis, therefore has volume $2\pi R \cdot \pi a^2 = 2\pi^2 R a^2$.

Rotating a curve rather than a region gives a surface, and the same chord argument yields the surface area $S = \int_a^b 2\pi f(x)\sqrt{1 + f'(x)^2}\,dx$. For the sphere, $f(x) = \sqrt{r^2 - x^2}$ and the integrand simplifies to the constant $2\pi r$, so $S = 4\pi r^2$: every slab of the sphere of thickness $\Delta x$ has the same area, another result of Archimedes.

At university level the single-variable recipe becomes the theory of [[multiple-integrals]]: the volume formula $\int A(x)\,dx$ is Fubini's theorem for $\iiint 1\,dV$, and the length formula is the start of the geometry of [[curves]].

- Displacement $\int v$ and distance $\int |v|$ are different; find where $v$ changes sign.
- Washers: $\pi(R^2 - r^2)$, not $\pi(R - r)^2$.
- Rotating about a line other than an axis (say $y = -1$) changes every radius: the radius is the distance to that line, here $f(x) + 1$.
- In pumping problems the distance lifted depends on the slice, and it is measured to wherever the liquid is delivered (the top of the tank, or a spout above it), not to the surface of the liquid.
- Units: a rate in litres per minute integrated over minutes gives litres. If the units of your integral do not match the quantity you want, the setup is wrong.

Every formula here is a single-variable shadow of a multivariable one: volumes and centres of mass become [[multiple-integrals]], work along a curved path becomes a line integral in [[vector-calculus]], and arc length is the starting point for [[curves]] and for [[parametric-polar|parametric and polar curves]]. For a continuous random variable (see [[distributions]]) the probability of an interval is an area under the density and the mean is a weighted average. Problems where one asks which curve minimises a length or an area lead to the [[calculus-of-variations]]. The evaluation techniques you need come from [[integration-techniques]].

1. Find the area of the region between $y = \sin x$ and $y = \cos x$ for $0 \le x \le \pi$.
2. The region under $y = \sqrt x$ on $[0,4]$ is rotated about the line $y = -1$. Set up and evaluate the volume.
3. Find the length of $y = \cosh x$ from $x = 0$ to $x = a$.
4. A conical tank, vertex down, has height 4 m and top radius 2 m and is full of water. Set up the integral for the work needed to pump all the water over the top edge.

entry.sum: A parametric curve gives both coordinates as functions of a parameter, $(x(t), y(t))$, which lets a curve loop, cross itself and record how it is traced; polar coordinates locate a point by its distance $r$ from the origin and its angle $\theta$. Calculus carries over through the chain rule: slopes are ratios of rates, $dy/dx = \dot y/\dot x$, and areas in polar coordinates are swept out by thin sectors, $\tfrac12 r^2\,d\theta$.
key: x = r\cos\theta,\quad y = r\sin\theta, \qquad A = \frac12\int_\alpha^\beta r(\theta)^2\,d\theta
entry.why: Motion is naturally parametric (position as a function of time), and many curves with rotational symmetry, from spirals and roses to planetary orbits $r = \ell/(1 + e\cos\theta)$, have simple polar equations but messy Cartesian ones.

links.note: Trajectories of projectiles and planets are parametric curves, and Kepler's second law says a planet's polar area rate $\tfrac12 r^2\dot\theta$ is constant.
The polar form $re^{i\theta}$ of a complex number is polar coordinates in the plane, and contour integrals are taken along parametrised curves.

refs: Stewart, Calculus: Early Transcendentals
Apostol, Calculus, Vol. 1

blocks.body:
The graph of a function $y = f(x)$ meets each vertical line at most once, so it cannot draw a circle, a figure eight, or the path of a pebble stuck in a rolling bicycle tyre. Two ideas remove this limitation. A parametric curve describes a point moving in time, with both coordinates given as functions of the time. Polar coordinates describe a point by how far away it is and in which direction, which suits anything that spins or spirals.

This page shows how to sketch such curves and how to do calculus with them: slopes, tangent lines, lengths and areas. Everything rests on the chain rule from [[derivative|the derivative]] and on the [[trig|trigonometric functions]].

blocks.title: Parametric curves
blocks.body:
A parametric curve is a pair of functions $x = x(t)$, $y = y(t)$ for $t$ in an interval. Think of $t$ as time and $(x(t), y(t))$ as the position of a moving point. The same set of points can be traced in many ways: $(\cos t, \sin t)$ and $(\cos 2t, \sin 2t)$ for $0 \le t \le 2\pi$ both give the unit circle, but the second goes round twice, twice as fast. Some standard examples:

- the line through $P$ in direction $v$: $P + tv$;
- the ellipse $x = a\cos t$, $y = b\sin t$, since then $x^2/a^2 + y^2/b^2 = 1$;
- the cycloid $x = r(t - \sin t)$, $y = r(1 - \cos t)$, traced by a point on the rim of a wheel of radius $r$ rolling along the $x$-axis: after turning through angle $t$ the wheel's centre is at $(rt, r)$ and the point sits $r$ units from the centre, rotated back by angle $t$.

To sketch a parametric curve, tabulate a few values. For $x = t^2$, $y = t^3 - 3t$:

$t$: $-2, -1, 0, 1, 2$; $x$: $4, 1, 0, 1, 4$; $y$: $-2, 2, 0, -2, 2$.

The curve comes in from the lower right ($y \to -\infty$ as $t \to -\infty$), rises to $(1, 2)$, passes through the origin, dips to $(1, -2)$ and leaves to the upper right, crossing itself at $(3, 0)$ where $t = \pm\sqrt3$. Eliminating $t$ is sometimes possible (here $y^2 = x(x-3)^2$) but loses the direction of travel.

blocks.title: Slopes and tangents
blocks.body:
If $x(t)$ and $y(t)$ are differentiable and $x'(t) \ne 0$, then near $t$ the curve is the graph of a function $y$ of $x$, and the chain rule $\frac{dy}{dt} = \frac{dy}{dx}\cdot\frac{dx}{dt}$ gives

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{y'(t)}{x'(t)}.$$

So horizontal tangents occur where $y' = 0$ (and $x' \ne 0$), vertical tangents where $x' = 0$ (and $y' \ne 0$). If both vanish the point needs separate attention; the cycloid has sharp cusps on the ground at $t = 0, 2\pi, \dots$, where $x' = r(1 - \cos t)$ and $y' = r\sin t$ are both zero.

The second derivative is the derivative of $dy/dx$ with respect to $x$, so apply the same rule to the function $m(t) = y'(t)/x'(t)$:

$$\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{m'(t)}{x'(t)}.$$

A common slip is to write $y''(t)/x''(t)$; that is wrong in general.

The vector $(x'(t), y'(t))$ is the velocity of the moving point. It points along the tangent, and its length is the speed.

blocks.title: Arc length
blocks.body:
Over a short time $\Delta t$ the point moves by about $(x'\Delta t, y'\Delta t)$, a distance $\sqrt{x'^2 + y'^2}\,\Delta t$. Adding these (compare [[integral-applications]]) gives the length of the path traced for $a \le t \le b$:

$$L = \int_a^b \sqrt{x'(t)^2 + y'(t)^2}\,dt.$$

This is distance travelled, so a curve traced twice is counted twice. For one arch of the cycloid, $$x'^2 + y'^2 = r^2\bigl((1-\cos t)^2 + \sin^2 t\bigr) = 2r^2(1 - \cos t) = 4r^2\sin^2(t/2)$$, so

$$L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2r\sin(t/2)\,dt = 8r.$$

The arch is exactly four times the diameter of the wheel, a fact found by Christopher Wren in the 17th century. The area under the arch is $$\int y\,dx = \int_0^{2\pi} r(1-\cos t)\cdot r(1 - \cos t)\,dt = 3\pi r^2$$, three times the area of the wheel.

blocks.title: Polar coordinates
blocks.body:
A point $P$ in the plane has polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$ if $P = (r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta)$. For $r > 0$, $r$ is the distance from the origin $O$ and $\theta$ is the angle from the positive $x$-axis to the ray $OP$. Conversely $r^2 = x^2 + y^2$ and $\tan\theta = y/x$ (with the quadrant chosen correctly).

Polar coordinates are not unique: $(r, \theta)$, $(r, \theta + 2\pi)$ and $(-r, \theta + \pi)$ all name the same point, and the origin is $(0, \theta)$ for every $\theta$. Negative $r$ is allowed and means 'go backwards along the ray'.

blocks.title: Polar graphs
blocks.body:
A polar curve $r = f(\theta)$ is the parametric curve $x = f(\theta)\cos\theta$, $y = f(\theta)\sin\theta$. To sketch it, imagine a searchlight sweeping anticlockwise from the origin and mark the point at distance $f(\theta)$ along the beam.

- $r = c$ is a circle of radius $c$; $\theta = c$ is a line through the origin.
- $r = 2a\cos\theta$ is a circle through the origin: multiplying by $r$ gives $x^2 + y^2 = 2ax$, that is $(x-a)^2 + y^2 = a^2$.
- $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ is a cardioid (heart shape). The values $\theta = 0, \pi/2, \pi$ give $r = 2, 1, 0$: the curve starts at $(2,0)$, passes $(0,1)$ and comes into the origin, then returns symmetrically below the axis.
- $r = \cos 2\theta$ is a four-petalled rose. As $\theta$ goes from $-\pi/4$ to $\pi/4$, $r$ rises from 0 to 1 and back, tracing the petal on the positive $x$-axis. Where $r < 0$ (for example $\pi/4 < \theta < 3\pi/4$) the point is drawn in the opposite direction, which produces the petals on the $y$-axis. In general $r = \cos k\theta$ has $k$ petals for odd $k$ and $2k$ for even $k$.
- $r = \theta$ ($\theta \ge 0$) is the spiral of Archimedes; successive turns are $2\pi$ apart.

Writing the curve as a parametric curve gives the slope. With $r' = dr/d\theta$,

$$\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{r'\sin\theta + r\cos\theta}{r'\cos\theta - r\sin\theta}.$$

At a point where the curve passes through the origin ($r = 0$, $r' \ne 0$) this reduces to $\tan\theta$: the curve leaves the origin along the ray $\theta$.

blocks.title: Area in polar coordinates
blocks.body:
If $f$ is continuous and nonnegative and $0 \le \beta - \alpha \le 2\pi$, the region swept by the ray from the origin to the curve $r = f(\theta)$, for $\alpha \le \theta \le \beta$, has area

$$A = \frac12\int_\alpha^\beta f(\theta)^2\,d\theta.$$

blocks.title: Why the formula holds
blocks.body: A circular sector of radius $r$ and angle $\Delta\theta$ has area $\frac12 r^2\Delta\theta$ (it is the fraction $\Delta\theta/2\pi$ of the disc $\pi r^2$). Cut $[\alpha, \beta]$ into $n$ small angles. On the $i$-th, let $m_i$ and $M_i$ be the least and greatest values of $f$. The piece of the region in that angle contains the sector of radius $m_i$ and lies inside the sector of radius $M_i$, so the area lies between $\sum \frac12 m_i^2\Delta\theta$ and $\sum \frac12 M_i^2 \Delta\theta$. These are lower and upper Riemann sums for $\frac12 f^2$ (see [[riemann-integral]]), and both tend to $\frac12\int_\alpha^\beta f^2\,d\theta$ as the angles shrink, because a continuous function is integrable.

blocks.title: Polar length and an area formula for any closed curve
blocks.body:
Using $x = r\cos\theta$, $y = r\sin\theta$ in the parametric length formula, the cross terms cancel and $x'^2 + y'^2 = r^2 + r'^2$, so

$$L = \int_\alpha^\beta \sqrt{r^2 + r'^2}\,d\theta.$$

For the cardioid $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ we get $r^2 + r'^2 = 2 + 2\cos\theta = 4\cos^2(\theta/2)$, and $L = \int_0^{2\pi} 2|\cos(\theta/2)|\,d\theta = 8$. Its area is $\frac12\int_0^{2\pi}(1+\cos\theta)^2\,d\theta = \frac{3\pi}{2}$.

The polar area formula also has a parametric version. If a curve $(x(t), y(t))$ moves around the origin, its angle $\theta(t)$ satisfies $\theta' = (xy' - yx')/(x^2 + y^2)$ (differentiate $\tan\theta = y/x$), so $\frac12 r^2\,d\theta = \frac12(xy' - yx')\,dt$. For a simple closed curve traced once anticlockwise,

$$A = \frac12\oint (x\,dy - y\,dx) = \frac12\int_a^b \bigl(x(t)y'(t) - y(t)x'(t)\bigr)\,dt.$$

We derived it for curves that every ray from the origin meets once; in fact it holds for every simple closed curve, which is a special case of Green's theorem in [[vector-calculus]].

blocks.title: Loop of a parametric curve
blocks.body: For the curve $x = t^2$, $y = t^3 - 3t$: (a) find the points with horizontal or vertical tangents; (b) find the two tangent lines at the self-crossing $(3,0)$; (c) decide where the curve is concave up; (d) find the area of the loop.
blocks.solution:
(a) $x' = 2t$ and $y' = 3t^2 - 3$. Horizontal tangents where $t = \pm1$: the points $(1, -2)$ and $(1, 2)$. Vertical tangent where $t = 0$: the origin.

(b) $dy/dx = (3t^2 - 3)/(2t)$. At $t = \sqrt3$ this is $6/(2\sqrt3) = \sqrt3$, and at $t = -\sqrt3$ it is $-\sqrt3$. The tangents are $y = \pm\sqrt3(x - 3)$.

(c) $m(t) = \frac32 t - \frac{3}{2t}$, so $m'(t) = \frac32 + \frac{3}{2t^2}$ and $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = \frac{m'(t)}{2t} = \frac{3(t^2+1)}{4t^3}$. This is positive for $t > 0$ and negative for $t < 0$: the half traced for $t > 0$ (from the origin down through $(1, -2)$, back through the crossing and off to the upper right) is concave up, and its mirror image, traced for $t < 0$, is concave down.

(d) The loop is traced for $-\sqrt3 \le t \le \sqrt3$. The area enclosed is $\left|\int y\,dx\right| = \left|\int_{-\sqrt3}^{\sqrt3}(t^3 - 3t)\,2t\,dt\right| = \left|\frac{36\sqrt3}{5} - 12\sqrt3\right| = \frac{24\sqrt3}{5}$.

blocks.title: Inside one circle, outside a cardioid
blocks.body: Find the area of the region inside $r = 3\cos\theta$ and outside $r = 1 + \cos\theta$. Also find the slope of the cardioid at $\theta = \pi/2$.
blocks.solution:
The curves meet where $3\cos\theta = 1 + \cos\theta$, so $\cos\theta = \frac12$ and $\theta = \pm\pi/3$. Between these angles the circle is further out. The area is the difference of two polar areas over the same angles:

$$\frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\bigl(9\cos^2\theta - (1+\cos\theta)^2\bigr)\,d\theta = \frac12\int_{-\pi/3}^{\pi/3}\bigl(8\cos^2\theta - 2\cos\theta - 1\bigr)\,d\theta.$$

Using $8\cos^2\theta = 4 + 4\cos 2\theta$, the integral is $\frac{8\pi}{3} + 2\sqrt3 - 2\sqrt3 - \frac{2\pi}{3} = 2\pi$, so the area is $\pi$.

For the slope, $r = 1$ and $r' = -\sin\theta = -1$ at $\theta = \pi/2$, so $dy/dx = \frac{(-1)(1) + (1)(0)}{(-1)(0) - (1)(1)} = 1$.

blocks.title: The astroid
blocks.body: The astroid is $x = \cos^3 t$, $y = \sin^3 t$, $0 \le t \le 2\pi$, a four-cusped star whose Cartesian equation is $x^{2/3} + y^{2/3} = 1$. (It is also the envelope of a ladder of length 1 sliding with its ends on the two axes.) Find its length and the area it encloses.
blocks.solution:
$x' = -3\cos^2 t\sin t$ and $y' = 3\sin^2 t\cos t$, so $x'^2 + y'^2 = 9\sin^2 t\cos^2 t$ and the speed is $3|\sin t\cos t|$. By symmetry the length is four times the first-quadrant arc:

$$L = 4\int_0^{\pi/2} 3\sin t\cos t\,dt = 4\cdot\frac32 = 6.$$

For the area use $\frac12\int(xy' - yx')\,dt$: here $xy' - yx' = 3\sin^2 t\cos^4 t + 3\sin^4 t\cos^2 t = 3\sin^2 t\cos^2 t$. Since $\sin^2 t\cos^2 t = \frac18(1 - \cos 4t)$, its integral over $[0, 2\pi]$ is $\pi/4$, and

$$A = \frac12\cdot 3\cdot\frac{\pi}{4} = \frac{3\pi}{8}.$$

The astroid encloses less than half the area of the unit circle it is inscribed in, although its four cusps touch that circle.

blocks.body:
- $\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}$ is not $y''(t)/x''(t)$; differentiate $dy/dx$ with respect to $t$ and divide by $x'(t)$.
- Polar area integrals need the right angle range. For $r = \cos 2\theta$, integrating $\frac12 r^2$ over $[0, 2\pi]$ gives the total area $\pi/2$ of all four petals; over $[0, \pi]$ you get only half of it. For $r = \cos 3\theta$ the three petals are traced once on $[0, \pi]$ and twice on $[0, 2\pi]$.
- Intersection points of polar curves may be missed by solving $f(\theta) = g(\theta)$: the curves may meet at the origin at different angles, or where one uses $(r,\theta)$ and the other $(-r, \theta + \pi)$. Sketch first.
- Area between polar curves is $\frac12\int(f^2 - g^2)$, not $\frac12\int(f - g)^2$.
- Arc length counts retracing: integrate only over one traversal.

Parametric curves are the starting point for the differential geometry of [[curves]], where the speed is normalised away and the curvature and the Frenet frame describe how the curve bends. In three dimensions the same formulas describe paths in space and line integrals in [[vector-calculus]], and polar coordinates grow into cylindrical and spherical coordinates for [[multiple-integrals]]. The [[conic-sections]] have the single polar equation $r = \ell/(1 + e\cos\theta)$ with the focus at the origin, which is how they appear as planetary orbits. Polar form is also the geometric meaning of multiplication of [[complex-numbers]].

1. Eliminate the parameter from $x = 1 + 2\cos t$, $y = 3\sin t - 1$ and identify the curve.
2. Find the points on the cardioid $r = 1 + \cos\theta$ where the tangent is horizontal.
3. Find the area inside one petal of $r = \sin 3\theta$.
4. Show that the length of $r = e^{\theta}$ for $T \le \theta \le 0$ is $\sqrt2\,(1 - e^T)$, and explain why the length stays finite as $T \to -\infty$ even though the spiral winds around the origin infinitely often.

Apostol, Calculus, Vol. 1

entry.sum: A system of linear differential equations $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x + \mathbf g(t)$ describes several quantities whose rates of change depend linearly on all of them. For a constant matrix $A$, each eigenvector $\mathbf v$ with eigenvalue $\lambda$ gives a solution $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ that simply grows or shrinks along a fixed direction, and every solution of the homogeneous system $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ is $e^{At}\mathbf x(0)$.
key: \mathbf x' = A\mathbf x,\quad A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v \;\Longrightarrow\; \mathbf x(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v
\mathbf x(t) = e^{At}\mathbf x(0) = \sum_i c_i e^{\lambda_i t}\mathbf v_i \quad (A \text{ diagonalisable})
entry.why: Coupled oscillators, electrical networks, compartment models in pharmacology and chemistry, and the linearisation of any nonlinear system near an equilibrium all lead to $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$, and the eigenvalues of $A$ decide growth, decay and oscillation.

links.note: Small vibrations of coupled masses and springs decompose into independent normal modes, whose angular frequencies are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $M^{-1}K$ ($M$ the mass matrix, $K$ the stiffness matrix).
The transition probabilities of a finite-state continuous-time Markov chain with generator $Q$ solve the linear system $P' = PQ$, so $P(t) = e^{tQ}$.
The eigenvalues of a linear system classify its equilibrium as a node, saddle, spiral or centre, the basic picture of local dynamics.

refs: Boyce, DiPrima & Meade, Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems
Strang, Introduction to Linear Algebra
Hirsch, Smale & Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos

blocks.body:
Two tanks of brine are connected by pipes; salt flows from each into the other at a rate proportional to the amount present. Two masses on a line are joined by springs; each one's acceleration depends on where both are. In both cases there are several unknown functions, and the derivative of each depends on all of them. A single equation like $y' = ky$ is no longer enough: we need a system.

The good news is that linear systems have a complete theory, and it is the theory of [[eigen|eigenvalues and eigenvectors]] in disguise. The aim of this page is to find all solutions of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ for a constant matrix $A$, to understand the three cases (real, complex and repeated eigenvalues), and to handle a forcing term.

blocks.title: From equations to a matrix
blocks.body:
A first-order linear system in $n$ unknowns $x_1(t), \dots, x_n(t)$ is

$$\mathbf x'(t) = A(t)\mathbf x(t) + \mathbf g(t),$$

where $\mathbf x = (x_1, \dots, x_n)^T$, $A(t)$ is an $n\times n$ matrix and $\mathbf g(t)$ a vector. It is homogeneous if $\mathbf g = 0$. On this page $A$ is usually constant.

Any linear equation of order $n$ turns into such a system (see [[ode-linear]]). For $y'' + py' + qy = 0$ set $x_1 = y$ and $x_2 = y'$; then $x_1' = x_2$ and $x_2' = -qx_1 - px_2$, so

$$\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2\end{pmatrix}' = \begin{pmatrix} 0 & 1 \\ -q & -p\end{pmatrix}\begin{pmatrix} x_1 \\ x_2\end{pmatrix}.$$

Conversely, systems arise directly. Masses $m = 1$ at positions $x_1, x_2$ (measured from rest), joined to two walls and to each other by three identical springs of stiffness 1, satisfy $x_1'' = -2x_1 + x_2$ and $x_2'' = x_1 - 2x_2$.

blocks.title: Basic theory
blocks.body:
Let $A(t)$ and $\mathbf g(t)$ be continuous on an interval $I$, $t_0 \in I$ and $\mathbf x_0 \in \mathbb R^n$. Then:

1. The problem $\mathbf x' = A(t)\mathbf x + \mathbf g(t)$, $\mathbf x(t_0) = \mathbf x_0$ has exactly one solution, and it exists on all of $I$.
2. The solutions of the homogeneous system form a vector space of dimension $n$.
3. If $\mathbf x^{(1)}, \dots, \mathbf x^{(n)}$ are solutions of the homogeneous system and $W(t) = \det\bigl[\mathbf x^{(1)}(t) \cdots \mathbf x^{(n)}(t)\bigr]$ is their Wronskian, then $W(t) = W(t_0)\exp\int_{t_0}^t \operatorname{tr}A(s)\,ds$ (Abel–Liouville). In particular $W$ is either never zero (the solutions form a basis, called a fundamental set) or identically zero.

blocks.title: Proof of 2, assuming 1
blocks.body: Sums and scalar multiples of solutions of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ are solutions, because differentiation and multiplication by $A$ are linear; so the solutions form a vector space $S$. Define $E : S \to \mathbb R^n$ by $E(\mathbf x) = \mathbf x(t_0)$. This map is linear. It is onto, because by part 1 every initial vector $\mathbf x_0$ is the value at $t_0$ of some solution. It is one-to-one, because if $\mathbf x(t_0) = 0$ then $\mathbf x$ and the zero function solve the same initial value problem, so by uniqueness $\mathbf x = 0$. Hence $E$ is an isomorphism and $\dim S = n$ (see [[basis-dimension]]). The same argument shows that solutions are independent as functions exactly when their values at a single time are independent vectors, which is why $W(t_0) \ne 0$ at one point already forces $W \ne 0$ everywhere.

blocks.title: The eigenvalue method
blocks.body:
Try $\mathbf x(t) = e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ with a constant vector $\mathbf v \ne 0$. Then $\mathbf x' = \lambda e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ and $A\mathbf x = e^{\lambda t}A\mathbf v$, so this is a solution exactly when $A\mathbf v = \lambda\mathbf v$. Each eigenvector gives a solution that moves along a fixed line through the origin, growing if $\lambda > 0$ and decaying if $\lambda < 0$.

If $A$ has $n$ independent eigenvectors $\mathbf v_1, \dots, \mathbf v_n$ (for instance if its eigenvalues are distinct), these $n$ solutions have Wronskian $\det[\mathbf v_1\cdots\mathbf v_n] \ne 0$ at $t = 0$, so by the theorem the general solution is

$$\mathbf x(t) = c_1e^{\lambda_1t}\mathbf v_1 + \cdots + c_ne^{\lambda_nt}\mathbf v_n.$$

Another way to see this is to change variables. Writing $A = PDP^{-1}$ (see [[diagonalization]]) and $\mathbf y = P^{-1}\mathbf x$, the system becomes $\mathbf y' = D\mathbf y$, which is $n$ separate equations $y_i' = \lambda_iy_i$. Eigenvector coordinates decouple the system.

Complex eigenvalues. If $A$ is real and $\lambda = \alpha + i\beta$ with $\beta \ne 0$ has eigenvector $\mathbf v = \mathbf a + i\mathbf b$, then $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ is a complex solution, and since $A$ is real, its real and imaginary parts are separately real solutions:

$$e^{\alpha t}(\mathbf a\cos\beta t - \mathbf b\sin\beta t), \qquad e^{\alpha t}(\mathbf a\sin\beta t + \mathbf b\cos\beta t).$$

They rotate with angular frequency $\beta$ while growing or shrinking like $e^{\alpha t}$. The conjugate eigenvalue gives nothing new.

Repeated eigenvalues. If $\lambda$ is a double root of the characteristic polynomial but has only one independent eigenvector $\mathbf v$, a second solution is $e^{\lambda t}(t\mathbf v + \mathbf w)$, where $\mathbf w$ solves $(A - \lambda I)\mathbf w = \mathbf v$ (a generalised eigenvector; compare [[jordan]]). Substituting confirms it: the derivative is $e^{\lambda t}(\lambda t\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w + \mathbf v)$ and $A$ applied to $t\mathbf v + \mathbf w$ gives $\lambda t\mathbf v + \lambda\mathbf w + \mathbf v$.

blocks.title: Matrix exponential and fundamental matrix
blocks.body:
For a square matrix $A$,

$$e^{At} = I + tA + \frac{t^2A^2}{2!} + \frac{t^3A^3}{3!} + \cdots.$$

The series converges for every $t$, can be differentiated term by term to give $\frac{d}{dt}e^{At} = Ae^{At}$, and equals $I$ at $t = 0$. So $\mathbf x(t) = e^{At}\mathbf x_0$ is the solution with $\mathbf x(0) = \mathbf x_0$. More generally, any matrix $\Phi(t)$ whose columns form a fundamental set is a fundamental matrix, and $e^{At} = \Phi(t)\Phi(0)^{-1}$.

In practice: if $A = PDP^{-1}$ then $e^{At} = Pe^{Dt}P^{-1}$ with $e^{Dt} = \operatorname{diag}(e^{\lambda_it})$; if $A = \lambda I + N$ with $N^2 = 0$, then $e^{At} = e^{\lambda t}(I + tN)$, because $\lambda I$ commutes with $N$ and the series for $e^{Nt}$ stops after two terms.

blocks.title: Forcing terms
blocks.body:
For $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x + \mathbf g(t)$ the general solution is a particular solution plus the general homogeneous solution, exactly as for a single equation. If $\mathbf g = \mathbf b$ is constant and $A$ is invertible, the constant $\mathbf x^* = -A^{-1}\mathbf b$ is a particular solution (an equilibrium), and $\mathbf x - \mathbf x^*$ solves the homogeneous system.

In general, variation of parameters gives a formula. Look for $\mathbf x = e^{At}\mathbf c(t)$. Then $\mathbf x' = Ae^{At}\mathbf c + e^{At}\mathbf c'$, so we need $e^{At}\mathbf c' = \mathbf g$, that is $\mathbf c' = e^{-At}\mathbf g$. Integrating,

$$\mathbf x(t) = e^{At}\mathbf x_0 + \int_0^t e^{A(t-s)}\mathbf g(s)\,ds.$$

Each bit of forcing $\mathbf g(s)\,ds$ applied at time $s$ is carried forward by the homogeneous flow for the remaining time $t - s$, and the effects add up. For example, with $A = \begin{pmatrix}0 & 1\\ -1 & 0\end{pmatrix}$ we have $e^{Au} = \begin{pmatrix}\cos u & \sin u\\ -\sin u & \cos u\end{pmatrix}$, and for $\mathbf g = (0, 1)^T$, $\mathbf x_0 = 0$ the formula gives $\mathbf x(t) = \int_0^t(\sin u, \cos u)^T du = (1 - \cos t, \sin t)^T$. This is the system form of $y'' + y = 1$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$.

blocks.title: Real distinct eigenvalues
blocks.body: Solve $x' = x + y$, $y' = 4x + y$ with $x(0) = 2$, $y(0) = 0$, and describe what happens as $t \to \infty$.
blocks.solution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & 1\\ 4 & 1\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(1-\lambda)^2 - 4$, so $\lambda = 3$ and $\lambda = -1$. For $\lambda = 3$: $(A - 3I)\mathbf v = 0$ gives $-2v_1 + v_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf v = (1, 2)$. For $\lambda = -1$: $2v_1 + v_2 = 0$, so $\mathbf v = (1, -2)$. Hence

$$\mathbf x(t) = c_1e^{3t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\2\end{pmatrix} + c_2e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-2\end{pmatrix}.$$

At $t = 0$: $c_1 + c_2 = 2$ and $2c_1 - 2c_2 = 0$, so $c_1 = c_2 = 1$, and $x = e^{3t} + e^{-t}$, $y = 2e^{3t} - 2e^{-t}$.

As $t \to \infty$ the $e^{-t}$ part dies and the solution lines up with the direction $(1, 2)$, growing like $e^{3t}$. Only solutions starting exactly on the line through $(1,-2)$ decay. The origin is a saddle.

blocks.title: Complex eigenvalues: a decaying spiral
blocks.body: Find the general real solution of $x' = -x - 2y$, $y' = 2x - y$.
blocks.solution:
$A = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -2\\ 2 & -1\end{pmatrix}$ has characteristic polynomial $(\lambda + 1)^2 + 4$, so $\lambda = -1 \pm 2i$. For $\lambda = -1 + 2i$, the first row of $A - \lambda I$ is $(-2i, -2)$, so $\mathbf v = (1, -i) = (1, 0) + i(0, -1)$. Thus $\mathbf a = (1, 0)$ and $\mathbf b = (0, -1)$, and the two real solutions are

$$e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\cos 2t\\ \sin 2t\end{pmatrix}, \qquad e^{-t}\begin{pmatrix}\sin 2t\\ -\cos 2t\end{pmatrix}.$$

The general solution is $c_1$ times the first plus $c_2$ times the second. Every solution circles the origin anticlockwise with angular speed 2 while its distance from the origin shrinks like $e^{-t}$: a stable spiral. One can check this directly: $\frac{d}{dt}(x^2 + y^2) = 2x(-x - 2y) + 2y(2x - y) = -2(x^2 + y^2)$.

blocks.title: A repeated eigenvalue
blocks.body: Compute $e^{At}$ for $A = \begin{pmatrix}1 & -1\\ 1 & 3\end{pmatrix}$ and write down the general solution of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$.
blocks.solution:
The trace is 4 and the determinant is 4, so the characteristic polynomial is $(\lambda - 2)^2$. Put $N = A - 2I = \begin{pmatrix}-1 & -1\\ 1 & 1\end{pmatrix}$. Then $N^2 = 0$, so

$$e^{At} = e^{2t}(I + tN) = e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1 - t & -t\\ t & 1 + t\end{pmatrix}.$$

Only one eigenvector direction exists: $N\mathbf v = 0$ gives $\mathbf v = (1, -1)$. A generalised eigenvector with $N\mathbf w = \mathbf v$ is $\mathbf w = (-1, 0)$. The general solution is

$$c_1e^{2t}\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} + c_2e^{2t}\left(t\begin{pmatrix}1\\-1\end{pmatrix} + \begin{pmatrix}-1\\0\end{pmatrix}\right),$$

and the columns of $e^{At}$ are the particular choices with $\mathbf x(0) = (1,0)$ and $(0,1)$. The factor $t$ is the signature of a repeated eigenvalue without a full set of eigenvectors.

blocks.title: Three functions chasing each other
blocks.body: Functions $f, g, h$ satisfy $f' = g$, $g' = h$, $h' = f$, with $f(0) = 1$ and $g(0) = h(0) = 0$. Find $f$, and show that $f^3 + g^3 + h^3 - 3fgh = 1$ for all $t$.
blocks.solution:
The matrix of the system is the cyclic shift $A = \begin{pmatrix}0&1&0\\0&0&1\\1&0&0\end{pmatrix}$ with $A^3 = I$, so its eigenvalues are the cube roots of unity $1, \omega, \omega^2$, where $\omega = e^{2\pi i/3}$. Since $f''' = f$, $f$ is a combination of $e^t$, $e^{\omega t}$, $e^{\omega^2t}$, and the initial data $f(0) = 1$, $f'(0) = g(0) = 0$, $f''(0) = h(0) = 0$ give

$$f(t) = \frac{e^t + e^{\omega t} + e^{\omega^2t}}{3} = \frac{e^t + 2e^{-t/2}\cos\bigl(\tfrac{\sqrt3}{2}t\bigr)}{3}.$$

(Its derivatives at 0 are $\frac13(1 + \omega^k + \omega^{2k})$, which is 1 for $k = 0$ and 0 for $k = 1, 2$.)

For the identity, let $Q = f^3 + g^3 + h^3 - 3fgh$. Differentiating and using the equations,

$$Q' = 3f^2g + 3g^2h + 3h^2f - 3(g\cdot gh + f\cdot hh + fg\cdot f) = 0.$$

So $Q$ is constant, and $Q(0) = 1$. No formula for $f$, $g$, $h$ was needed for this part: finding a conserved quantity is often easier than solving.

blocks.body:
- An eigenvector solution is $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$, not $e^{\lambda t}$ times an arbitrary vector; the vector must be an eigenvector of that $\lambda$.
- With a repeated eigenvalue, $te^{\lambda t}\mathbf v$ alone is not a solution; the extra term $e^{\lambda t}\mathbf w$ is essential.
- $e^{A+B} = e^Ae^B$ only when $AB = BA$. In particular, for non-constant $A(t)$, $\exp\int A$ is generally not a solution.
- For complex eigenvalues, the real and imaginary parts of one complex solution already give two independent real solutions; the conjugate eigenvalue adds nothing new.
- The constant equilibrium $-A^{-1}\mathbf b$ needs $A$ invertible; if $0$ is an eigenvalue there may be no equilibrium at all, and a particular solution has to be found another way, for instance by variation of parameters.

For $2\times2$ systems, the signs of the eigenvalues give a picture of all solutions at once, classifying the origin as a saddle, node, spiral or centre; nonlinear systems look like their linearisation near an equilibrium. This is the subject of [[phase-plane]]. The matrix exponential reappears as the solution operator $e^{tQ}$ of continuous-time [[markov-chains]], and as the exponential map from [[lie-algebras]] to [[lie-groups]]. Large stiff systems are solved approximately by the methods of [[numerical-odes]], and separating variables in the [[heat-equation]] produces an infinite version of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ with a diagonal $A$.

1. Solve $x' = 2x + y$, $y' = x + 2y$ with $x(0) = 1$, $y(0) = 3$.
2. Find the normal modes and frequencies of the coupled masses $x_1'' = -2x_1 + x_2$, $x_2'' = x_1 - 2x_2$ by looking for solutions $\cos(\omega t)\mathbf v$.
3. Show that if every eigenvalue of $A$ has negative real part, every solution of $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ tends to $0$. (Treat the diagonalisable case first.)
4. Use the Abel–Liouville formula to compute the Wronskian of any two solutions of $\mathbf x' = \begin{pmatrix}1 & t\\ 0 & -3\end{pmatrix}\mathbf x$, up to a constant.

Hirsch, Smale & Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos

entry.sum: The Laplace transform $F(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$ turns a function of time into a function of a new variable $s$. Its key property is that differentiation becomes multiplication, $\mathcal L\{f'\} = sF(s) - f(0)$, so a linear differential equation with constant coefficients and its initial conditions becomes an algebraic equation for $F$, even when the forcing is switched on and off or is an impulse.
key: \mathcal L\{f'\} = sF(s) - f(0), \qquad \mathcal L\{f''\} = s^2F(s) - sf(0) - f'(0)
entry.why: Engineers analyse circuits, control systems and vibrations with it: the transfer function of a linear system is a Laplace transform, and the positions of its poles in the complex $s$-plane decide whether the system is stable.

links.note: Circuits and damped oscillators with switched or impulsive inputs are solved by transforming their equations of motion into algebra in $s$.
For a nonnegative random variable $X$ with density $f$, the transform $\mathbb E[e^{-sX}]$ is the Laplace transform of $f$, and the density of a sum of independent variables is a convolution.
The inverse transform is a contour integral along a vertical line in the complex plane, usually evaluated by residues at the poles of $F$.

refs: Boyce, DiPrima & Meade, Elementary Differential Equations and Boundary Value Problems
Schiff, The Laplace Transform: Theory and Applications
Widder, The Laplace Transform

blocks.body:
A mass on a spring is at rest. At time $\pi$ a motor starts pushing it with a constant force, and at time $2\pi$ the motor switches off. What does the mass do afterwards? The forcing is discontinuous, so solving the equation means solving it piece by piece and matching values and slopes at every switch. With several switches this is tedious and error-prone.

The Laplace transform handles such problems in one pass. It converts the differential equation, initial conditions included, into an algebraic equation; one solves that by algebra and partial fractions, then converts back with a table. The method assumes you know [[ode-linear|linear differential equations]] and [[improper-integrals]], since the transform is itself an improper integral.

blocks.title: Laplace transform
blocks.body:
For a function $f$ defined for $t \ge 0$, its Laplace transform is

$$F(s) = \mathcal L\{f\}(s) = \int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt = \lim_{A\to\infty}\int_0^A e^{-st}f(t)\,dt,$$

for those real $s$ (later also complex $s$) for which the limit exists. We say $f$ has exponential order $c$ if $|f(t)| \le Me^{ct}$ for all $t \ge T$, for some constants $M$ and $T$.

The factor $e^{-st}$ is a weight that discounts the far future; the larger $s$ is, the more the transform reflects the behaviour of $f$ near $t = 0$.

blocks.title: Existence
blocks.body: If $f$ is piecewise continuous on every interval $[0, A]$ and has exponential order $c$, then $\mathcal L\{f\}(s)$ exists for every $s > c$, and $F(s) \to 0$ as $s \to \infty$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body: On $[0, T]$ the integrand is piecewise continuous, hence integrable. For $t \ge T$, $|e^{-st}f(t)| \le Me^{-(s-c)t}$, and $\int_T^\infty Me^{-(s-c)t}\,dt$ converges when $s > c$, so the integral converges absolutely by the comparison test. For the limit, write $|f| \le K$ on $[0,T]$; then $|F(s)| \le K/s + M/(s - c)$ for $s > c$, which tends to 0.

blocks.title: A small table and how it is made
Transform of a derivative
blocks.body:
If $f$ is continuous on $[0, \infty)$, of exponential order $c$, and $f'$ is piecewise continuous on every $[0,A]$, then for $s > c$

$$\mathcal L\{f'\}(s) = sF(s) - f(0).$$

Applying this twice, $\mathcal L\{f''\} = s^2F(s) - sf(0) - f'(0)$, when $f'$ also satisfies the hypotheses.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Integrate by parts on $[0, A]$ (on each piece where $f'$ is continuous; the boundary terms at interior break points cancel because $f$ is continuous):

$$\int_0^A e^{-st}f'(t)\,dt = e^{-sA}f(A) - f(0) + s\int_0^A e^{-st}f(t)\,dt.$$

For large $A$, $|e^{-sA}f(A)| \le Me^{-(s-c)A} \to 0$ because $s > c$. Letting $A \to \infty$ gives $sF(s) - f(0)$.

blocks.title: Solving initial value problems
blocks.body:
The procedure for $ay'' + by' + cy = g(t)$ with given $y(0)$ and $y'(0)$:

1. Transform both sides, using the derivative rule; the initial conditions enter automatically.
2. Solve the resulting linear equation for $Y(s)$. It always has the form $Y = \frac{\text{(terms from initial data)} + G(s)}{as^2 + bs + c}$; the denominator is the characteristic polynomial.
3. Split $Y$ into partial fractions (see [[integration-techniques]]) and read off $y(t)$ from the table.

Take $y'' - y' - 2y = 0$, $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 0$. Step 1 gives $(s^2Y - s) - (sY - 1) - 2Y = 0$. Step 2 gives $Y = \frac{s-1}{(s-2)(s+1)}$. Step 3: $Y = \frac{1/3}{s-2} + \frac{2/3}{s+1}$, so $y = \frac13e^{2t} + \frac23e^{-t}$. One checks $y(0) = 1$ and $y'(0) = \frac23 - \frac23 = 0$.

The method is not faster than the characteristic-equation method for problems like this one. Its real advantage appears with discontinuous or impulsive forcing.

blocks.title: Step functions and the delta function
blocks.body:
The unit step at $c \ge 0$ is $u_c(t) = 0$ for $t < c$ and $u_c(t) = 1$ for $t \ge c$. Its transform is $e^{-cs}/s$, and more generally (second shift theorem)

$$\mathcal L\{u_c(t)f(t-c)\} = e^{-cs}F(s),$$

which follows from the substitution $\tau = t - c$ in the integral. The function $u_c(t)f(t - c)$ is $f$ delayed by $c$ and switched off before $c$. A pulse that is on during $[a, b)$ is $u_a - u_b$.

A sharp blow at time $c$ (a hammer strike, a sudden injection of charge) is modelled by the Dirac delta $\delta(t - c)$. It is not a function but the limit of pulses of height $1/\varepsilon$ on $[c, c + \varepsilon)$, each of total area 1. The transform of such a pulse is $e^{-cs}\frac{1 - e^{-\varepsilon s}}{\varepsilon s}$, which tends to $e^{-cs}$ as $\varepsilon \to 0$, so we set $\mathcal L\{\delta(t - c)\} = e^{-cs}$.

blocks.title: Convolution theorem
blocks.body:
For $f, g$ piecewise continuous and of exponential order, define the convolution $(f * g)(t) = \int_0^t f(\tau)g(t - \tau)\,d\tau$. Then

$$\mathcal L\{f * g\}(s) = F(s)\,G(s)$$

for all $s$ large enough that both transforms converge absolutely.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
$F(s)G(s) = \int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty e^{-s(\tau + u)}f(\tau)g(u)\,du\,d\tau$. In the inner integral substitute $t = \tau + u$, so $u = t - \tau$ runs from $\tau$ to $\infty$:

$$F(s)G(s) = \int_0^\infty\int_\tau^\infty e^{-st}f(\tau)g(t - \tau)\,dt\,d\tau.$$

The region is $0 \le \tau \le t < \infty$. The double integral converges absolutely (replace $f, g$ by $|f|, |g|$ and run the same computation), so the order of integration may be swapped (Fubini's theorem, see [[multiple-integrals]]). Integrating first over $\tau \in [0, t]$ gives $\int_0^\infty e^{-st}(f*g)(t)\,dt$.

blocks.title: Transfer functions
blocks.body: For the equation $ay'' + by' + cy = g$ with zero initial data, the transform gives $Y(s) = H(s)G(s)$ with $H(s) = 1/(as^2 + bs + c)$. The function $H$ is the transfer function, and its inverse transform $h(t)$ is the impulse response: the solution when $g = \delta(t)$. The convolution theorem then says $y = h * g$: the response to any input is a superposition of delayed impulse responses, one for each instant of forcing. If all poles of $H$ (the roots of $as^2 + bs + c$) have negative real part, $h(t)$ decays and bounded inputs give bounded outputs. This is the stability criterion used throughout control engineering.

blocks.title: A force switched on and off
blocks.body: Solve $y'' + y = g(t)$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$, where $g(t) = 1$ for $\pi \le t < 2\pi$ and $g(t) = 0$ otherwise. Describe the motion for $t > 2\pi$.
blocks.solution:
Here $g = u_\pi - u_{2\pi}$, so $(s^2 + 1)Y = \frac{e^{-\pi s} - e^{-2\pi s}}{s}$ and

$$Y = \bigl(e^{-\pi s} - e^{-2\pi s}\bigr)\frac{1}{s(s^2+1)}, \qquad \frac{1}{s(s^2+1)} = \frac1s - \frac{s}{s^2+1}.$$

The inverse of $\frac1s - \frac{s}{s^2+1}$ is $1 - \cos t$. By the second shift theorem,

$$y(t) = u_\pi(t)\bigl(1 - \cos(t - \pi)\bigr) - u_{2\pi}(t)\bigl(1 - \cos(t - 2\pi)\bigr) = u_\pi(t)(1 + \cos t) - u_{2\pi}(t)(1 - \cos t).$$

So $y = 0$ until $t = \pi$, then $y = 1 + \cos t$ while the force acts, and for $t \ge 2\pi$, $y = (1 + \cos t) - (1 - \cos t) = 2\cos t$. The mass is left oscillating with amplitude 2. Note that $y$ and $y'$ are continuous at both switching times, as they must be physically; the transform took care of the matching.

blocks.title: A hammer blow
blocks.body: A damped oscillator at rest is struck at time 2: $y'' + 2y' + 5y = \delta(t - 2)$, $y(0) = y'(0) = 0$. Find $y$.
blocks.solution:
Transforming, $(s^2 + 2s + 5)Y = e^{-2s}$. Complete the square: $s^2 + 2s + 5 = (s+1)^2 + 4$. By the first shift theorem $\frac{2}{(s+1)^2 + 4}$ is the transform of $e^{-t}\sin 2t$, so

$$Y = \frac12e^{-2s}\frac{2}{(s+1)^2 + 4}, \qquad y(t) = \tfrac12u_2(t)e^{-(t-2)}\sin\bigl(2(t - 2)\bigr).$$

The position is continuous at $t = 2$ but the velocity jumps from 0 to $\frac12\cdot 2 = 1$: a unit impulse changes momentum by 1 (the coefficient of $y''$ is 1).

blocks.title: Resonance by convolution
blocks.solution:
$Y = \frac{1}{(s^2+1)^2} = \frac{1}{s^2+1}\cdot\frac{1}{s^2+1}$, the product of two transforms of $\sin t$. By the convolution theorem,

$$y(t) = \int_0^t \sin\tau\,\sin(t - \tau)\,d\tau = \frac12\int_0^t\bigl(\cos(2\tau - t) - \cos t\bigr)\,d\tau = \frac{\sin t - t\cos t}{2}.$$

The term $-\frac12t\cos t$ grows without bound: forcing at the natural frequency of the oscillator produces resonance.

blocks.title: Integrals from transforms
blocks.body: Assuming the interchange of integrals is justified, show that $\int_0^\infty f(t)/t\,dt = \int_0^\infty F(s)\,ds$. Use it to find $\int_0^\infty \frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt$ and, for $0 < a < b$, $\int_0^\infty \frac{e^{-at} - e^{-bt}}{t}\,dt$.
blocks.solution:
$\int_0^\infty F(s)\,ds = \int_0^\infty\int_0^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt\,ds = \int_0^\infty f(t)\Bigl(\int_0^\infty e^{-st}ds\Bigr)dt = \int_0^\infty \frac{f(t)}{t}\,dt.$

With $f = \sin t$, $F(s) = \frac{1}{s^2+1}$, and $\int_0^\infty\frac{ds}{1+s^2} = \frac{\pi}{2}$. So $\int_0^\infty\frac{\sin t}{t}\,dt = \frac{\pi}{2}$. (Here the swap needs care because $\sin t/t$ is not absolutely integrable; it can be justified by inserting a factor $e^{-\varepsilon t}$ and letting $\varepsilon \to 0$.)

With $f = e^{-at} - e^{-bt}$, $F(s) = \frac{1}{s+a} - \frac{1}{s+b}$, and $\int_0^\infty F = \bigl[\ln\frac{s+a}{s+b}\bigr]_0^\infty = \ln\frac{b}{a}$.

blocks.title: The bigger picture
blocks.body:
Allowing $s = \sigma + i\omega$ to be complex, $F(\sigma + i\omega) = \int_0^\infty e^{-i\omega t}\bigl(e^{-\sigma t}f(t)\bigr)\,dt$ is the [[fourier-transform]] of the damped function $e^{-\sigma t}f(t)$ (set to 0 for $t < 0$). Inverting the Fourier transform gives the Bromwich inversion formula

$$f(t) = \frac{1}{2\pi i}\int_{\sigma - i\infty}^{\sigma + i\infty}e^{st}F(s)\,ds,$$

along any vertical line to the right of all singularities of $F$. For rational $F$ the integral is a sum of [[residues]] at the poles, and partial fractions are exactly this residue computation done by hand. A pole at $s = \lambda$ of order $k$ produces terms $t^je^{\lambda t}$ with $j < k$, which is why the roots of the characteristic polynomial reappear. The transform is also useful for systems: applied to $\mathbf x' = A\mathbf x$ it gives $(sI - A)\mathbf X = \mathbf x(0)$, so $\mathcal L\{e^{At}\} = (sI - A)^{-1}$ (compare [[ode-systems]]).

- The transform of a product is not the product of the transforms; products in $s$ correspond to convolutions in $t$.
- $\mathcal L\{f(t - c)\}$ is not $e^{-cs}F(s)$ unless $f(t-c)$ is switched off for $t < c$; the theorem is about $u_c(t)f(t - c)$. To transform $u_c(t)g(t)$, write $g(t) = f(t - c)$, i.e. use $f(t) = g(t + c)$.
- In $\mathcal L\{f''\} = s^2F - sf(0) - f'(0)$, the sign and the power of $s$ on each initial term matter; most mistakes in solved problems come from here.
- Not every function has a transform: $e^{t^2}$ grows too fast for any $s$.
- The delta function is defined by what it does inside integrals; statements like "$\delta(0) = \infty$" are not a definition.

The Laplace transform is one of a family of integral transforms: it is a damped one-sided [[fourier-transform]], and the substitution $x = e^{-t}$ turns the [[mellin]] transform used in analytic number theory into the two-sided version $\int_{-\infty}^\infty e^{-st}f(t)\,dt$. Its inversion is an exercise in [[residues]]. In probability, $\mathbb E[e^{-sX}]$ plays the role of the [[moment-generating]] function for nonnegative random variables. For first-order systems it turns [[ode-systems]] into linear algebra over rational functions of $s$, and it is also a standard tool for the [[heat-equation]] on a half-line, where transforming in time leaves an ordinary differential equation in space.

1. Find $\mathcal L\{t^2e^{-t}\}$ and $\mathcal L\{\cos^2 t\}$.
2. Solve $y' + 3y = u_1(t)$, $y(0) = 2$.
3. Solve $y'' + 4y = \delta(t - \pi)$, $y(0) = 1$, $y'(0) = 0$, and sketch the solution.
4. Show that the integral equation $y(t) = t + \int_0^t (t - \tau)\,y(\tau)\,d\tau$ has solution $y = \sinh t$.

entry.sum: When a linear differential equation has non-constant coefficients, one can look for a solution as a power series $y = \sum a_nx^n$: substituting turns the equation into a recurrence for the coefficients. Near an ordinary point this always works, and the series converges at least as far as the nearest singularity of the coefficients (complex singularities included); near a regular singular point the method of Frobenius uses $y = x^r\sum a_nx^n$, with $r$ fixed by the indicial equation.
key: y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0,\ p, q \text{ analytic at } x_0 \;\Longrightarrow\; y = \sum_{n\ge0} a_n(x - x_0)^n
entry.why: Many of the special functions of physics, such as Bessel functions for vibrating drums and Legendre polynomials for the hydrogen atom and gravitational potentials, are defined as series solutions of equations that cannot be solved in elementary terms.

links.note: Separating variables in Laplace's, the heat and the wave equations in polar or spherical coordinates produces Bessel and Legendre equations, solved by series.

The radius of convergence of a series solution is governed by the complex singularities of the coefficients, and the Frobenius method is the start of the theory of Fuchsian equations in the complex plane.

Coddington, An Introduction to Ordinary Differential Equations
Bender & Orszag, Advanced Mathematical Methods for Scientists and Engineers

blocks.body:
The equation $y'' + y = 0$ is solved by $\cos x$ and $\sin x$, but the innocent-looking $y'' - xy = 0$ (Airy's equation, which describes light near a caustic and a quantum particle in a constant field) has no solution in terms of elementary functions. What can we do? We can still compute the solution's Taylor coefficients, one after another, and often that is all we need: for numerical values, for qualitative behaviour, or as the definition of a new function.

This page develops the method for second-order [[ode-linear|linear equations]], using what you know about [[power-series]]: how far the series converges, what goes wrong at singular points, and how the method of Frobenius rescues the most important singular cases, including Bessel's equation.

blocks.title: The idea on a known example
blocks.body:
Look for a solution of $y'' + y = 0$ of the form $y = \sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$. Differentiating term by term, $y'' = \sum_{n\ge0}(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2}x^n$ (we shifted the index so both sums run over $x^n$). The equation says

$$\sum_{n\ge0}\bigl[(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} + a_n\bigr]x^n = 0,$$

and a power series is zero only if every coefficient is zero. So $a_{n+2} = -\frac{a_n}{(n+2)(n+1)}$. The free choices $a_0 = y(0)$ and $a_1 = y'(0)$ determine everything: $a_0 = 1$, $a_1 = 0$ gives $1 - \frac{x^2}{2!} + \frac{x^4}{4!} - \cdots = \cos x$, and $a_0 = 0$, $a_1 = 1$ gives $\sin x$. We recovered the two solutions without knowing them in advance.

The general recipe: substitute, shift indices so every term has $x^n$, equate coefficients to get a recurrence, and solve it starting from $a_0$, $a_1$.

blocks.title: Airy's and Legendre's equations
blocks.body:
Airy's equation $y'' = xy$. Now $xy = \sum a_{n-1}x^n$ (starting at $n = 1$), so comparing coefficients: $2a_2 = 0$ and $(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} = a_{n-1}$ for $n \ge 1$. The coefficients go up in steps of three. Starting from $a_0 = 1, a_1 = 0$:

$$y_1 = 1 + \frac{x^3}{6} + \frac{x^6}{180} + \frac{x^9}{12960} + \cdots,$$

and from $a_0 = 0, a_1 = 1$:

$$y_2 = x + \frac{x^4}{12} + \frac{x^7}{504} + \cdots.$$

For $x > 0$ almost every solution grows very fast (where $y > 0$ the equation makes $y'' > 0$, pushing the curve further up); only one solution up to a constant factor, the Airy function $\operatorname{Ai}$, decays instead. For $x < 0$ the equation reads $y'' + |x|y = 0$, an oscillator whose frequency increases with $|x|$, and the solutions oscillate.

Legendre's equation $(1 - x^2)y'' - 2xy' + \alpha(\alpha + 1)y = 0$. The same procedure gives

$$a_{n+2} = -\frac{(\alpha - n)(\alpha + n + 1)}{(n+2)(n+1)}a_n.$$

If $\alpha = m$ is a nonnegative integer, the factor $\alpha - n$ vanishes at $n = m$, so one of the two series stops: there is a polynomial solution of degree $m$. Normalised so that its value at $1$ is $1$, it is the Legendre polynomial $P_m$; for instance $P_0 = 1$, $P_1 = x$, $P_2 = \frac12(3x^2 - 1)$, $P_3 = \frac12(5x^3 - 3x)$. These are used for expansions on the interval $[-1, 1]$ and on the sphere.

blocks.title: Ordinary and singular points
blocks.body:
Write the equation as $y'' + p(x)y' + q(x)y = 0$ (divide by the leading coefficient). A point $x_0$ is an ordinary point if $p$ and $q$ are analytic at $x_0$, that is, equal to convergent power series in $x - x_0$ near $x_0$. Otherwise $x_0$ is a singular point.

For rational coefficients this just means the denominators (after cancelling common factors) do not vanish at $x_0$. For Legendre's equation $p = -2x/(1 - x^2)$ and $q = \alpha(\alpha+1)/(1-x^2)$, so $x = \pm1$ are singular and all other points are ordinary.

blocks.title: Series solutions at an ordinary point
blocks.body: If $p(x) = \sum p_kx^k$ and $q(x) = \sum q_kx^k$ both converge for $|x| < R$, then for every $a_0, a_1$ there is a unique solution $y = \sum a_nx^n$ with $y(0) = a_0$, $y'(0) = a_1$, and its series also converges for $|x| < R$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Substituting and comparing coefficients of $x^n$ gives

$$(n+2)(n+1)a_{n+2} = -\sum_{k=0}^n\bigl[(n-k+1)p_ka_{n-k+1} + q_ka_{n-k}\bigr],$$

which determines $a_2, a_3, \dots$ from $a_0, a_1$. It remains to show that the series converges for $|x| < R$; then term-by-term differentiation and multiplication of power series are valid and the series really is a solution (uniqueness follows from the uniqueness theorem for linear equations, or directly from the recurrence).

Fix $0 < \rho < R$. Since $\sum p_k\rho^k$ converges, its terms are bounded, so there is $M > 0$ with $|p_k|, |q_k| \le M\rho^{-k}$ for all $k$. Define a comparison sequence by $b_0 = |a_0| + 1$, $b_1 = |a_1| + 1$ and

$$(n+2)(n+1)b_{n+2} = M\sum_{k=0}^n\bigl[(n-k+1)b_{n-k+1} + b_{n-k}\bigr]\rho^{-k}.$$

By induction $|a_n| \le b_n$ and $b_n > 0$ for all $n$. Call the sum on the right $S_n$. Splitting off the $k = 0$ term and factoring $\rho^{-1}$ from the rest shows $S_n = (n+1)b_{n+1} + b_n + \rho^{-1}S_{n-1}$, and $MS_{n-1} = (n+1)n\,b_{n+1}$. Therefore

$$\frac{b_{n+2}}{b_{n+1}} = \frac{\rho^{-1}n(n+1) + M(n+1) + Mb_n/b_{n+1}}{(n+2)(n+1)}.$$

Since $MS_{n-1}$ contains the term $Mn\,b_n$, we have $(n+1)n\,b_{n+1} \ge Mn\,b_n$, so $Mb_n/b_{n+1} \le n+1$. Hence the right side tends to $1/\rho$, and by the ratio test $\sum b_nx^n$ converges for $|x| < \rho$. By comparison so does $\sum a_nx^n$. As $\rho < R$ was arbitrary, the radius of convergence is at least $R$.

blocks.title: How far does the series reach?
blocks.body: The theorem is about the radius of convergence of $p$ and $q$, which is the distance to their nearest singularity in the complex plane. For Legendre's equation the singularities are $\pm1$, so the series converge on $(-1, 1)$, and for non-integer $\alpha$ they genuinely diverge at $x = \pm1$. For $(1 + x^2)y'' + y = 0$, nothing goes wrong on the real line, yet the theorem only guarantees radius $1$ about $x = 0$, because $1 + x^2$ vanishes at $x = \pm i$. For Airy's equation $p = 0$ and $q = -x$ are polynomials, $R = \infty$, and the series converge for all $x$.

blocks.title: Regular singular points and the Euler equation
blocks.body:
Near a singular point solutions may blow up or fail to be smooth, and no power series can capture that. The model case is the Euler equation

$$x^2y'' + \alpha xy' + \beta y = 0, \qquad x > 0.$$

Trying $y = x^r$ gives $r(r-1) + \alpha r + \beta = 0$. Two distinct real roots give $x^{r_1}$ and $x^{r_2}$; a double root $r$ gives $x^r$ and $x^r\ln x$; complex roots $\lambda \pm i\mu$ give $x^\lambda\cos(\mu\ln x)$ and $x^\lambda\sin(\mu\ln x)$. (The substitution $x = e^t$ turns the Euler equation into one with constant coefficients, which explains this list.) So solutions can behave like $x^{-1/2}$, $\sqrt x$ or $\ln x$ at $0$: singular, but in a controlled way.

A singular point $x_0 = 0$ is regular if $xp(x)$ and $x^2q(x)$ are analytic at $0$, so the equation is a perturbation of an Euler equation with $\alpha = p_0 = \lim xp(x)$ and $\beta = q_0 = \lim x^2q(x)$. The method of Frobenius tries

$$y = x^r\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n, \qquad a_0 \ne 0.$$

The lowest power of $x$ gives the indicial equation $r(r-1) + p_0r + q_0 = 0$, and the higher powers give a recurrence for $a_n$.

blocks.title: Frobenius' theorem
blocks.body:
Let $0$ be a regular singular point, with $xp(x)$ and $x^2q(x)$ analytic for $|x| < R$, and let the indicial equation have real roots $r_1 \ge r_2$. Then on $0 < x < R$ there are solutions of the following forms, all the series converging for $|x| < R$:

1. There is a solution $y_1 = x^{r_1}\sum_{n\ge0}a_nx^n$ with $a_0 = 1$.
2. If $r_1 - r_2$ is not an integer, there is a second solution $y_2 = x^{r_2}\sum_{n\ge0}c_nx^n$, $c_0 = 1$.
3. If $r_1 = r_2$, a second solution is $y_2 = y_1\ln x + x^{r_1}\sum_{n\ge1}c_nx^n$.
4. If $r_1 - r_2$ is a positive integer, a second solution is $y_2 = ay_1\ln x + x^{r_2}\sum_{n\ge0}c_nx^n$, $c_0 = 1$, where the constant $a$ may or may not be zero.

In case 3 the indicial equation supplies only one exponent, and in case 4 the recurrence for the smaller root can break down, because the coefficient of $c_n$, namely $(n + r_2)(n + r_2 - 1) + p_0(n + r_2) + q_0$, vanishes at $n = r_1 - r_2$. The logarithmic term makes up for the missing series solution.

blocks.title: Two Frobenius solutions with closed forms
blocks.body: Solve $2xy'' + y' + y = 0$ near $x = 0$ by the method of Frobenius, and identify the two solutions.
blocks.solution:
Dividing by $2x$: $p = \frac{1}{2x}$ and $q = \frac{1}{2x}$, so $xp = \frac12$ and $x^2q = \frac x2$ are analytic: $0$ is a regular singular point with $p_0 = \frac12$, $q_0 = 0$. The indicial equation $r(r-1) + \frac r2 = 0$ has roots $r = 0$ and $r = \frac12$, which do not differ by an integer.

Substituting $y = \sum a_nx^{n+r}$: the terms $2xy''$ and $y'$ contribute $(n+r)(2n + 2r - 1)a_nx^{n+r-1}$ and $y$ contributes $a_{n-1}x^{n+r-1}$ after a shift. So

$$a_n = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{(n+r)(2n+2r-1)}.$$

For $r = 0$: $a_n = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{n(2n-1)} = -\frac{2a_{n-1}}{(2n)(2n-1)}$, so $a_n = \frac{(-1)^n2^n}{(2n)!}$ and

$$y_1 = \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^n(2x)^n}{(2n)!} = \cos\sqrt{2x}.$$

For $r = \frac12$: $a_n = -\frac{a_{n-1}}{n(2n+1)} = -\frac{2a_{n-1}}{(2n+1)(2n)}$, so $a_n = \frac{(-1)^n2^n}{(2n+1)!}$ and

$$y_2 = x^{1/2}\sum_{n\ge0}\frac{(-1)^n(2x)^n}{(2n+1)!} = \frac{\sin\sqrt{2x}}{\sqrt2}.$$

Indeed the substitution $x = u^2/2$ turns the equation into $y'' + y = 0$ in $u$. Note that $y_2$ is not differentiable at $0$: such behaviour is exactly what Frobenius' method allows.

blocks.title: Bessel's equation
blocks.body:
Bessel's equation of order $
u \ge 0$ is $x^2y'' + xy' + (x^2 - 
u^2)y = 0$. Find the indicial roots and the Frobenius solution for the larger root when $
u = 0$. What happens when $
u =  rac12$?
blocks.solution:
Here $p_0 = 1$ and $q_0 = -\nu^2$, so the indicial equation is $r^2 - \nu^2 = 0$ and $r = \pm\nu$.

Take $\nu = 0$, so $r = 0$ is a double root. With $y = \sum a_nx^n$, the terms $x^2y'' + xy'$ give $n^2a_nx^n$ and $x^2y$ gives $a_{n-2}x^n$. So $n^2a_n = -a_{n-2}$, $a_1 = 0$, and all odd coefficients vanish. With $a_0 = 1$, $a_{2k} = \frac{(-1)^k}{4^k(k!)^2}$:

$$J_0(x) = 1 - \frac{x^2}{4} + \frac{x^4}{64} - \frac{x^6}{2304} + \cdots = \sum_{k\ge0}\frac{(-1)^k}{(k!)^2}\Bigl(\frac x2\Bigr)^{2k}.$$

The radius is infinite. Since the indicial root is double, the second solution contains $J_0(x)\ln x$ and is unbounded at $0$ (case 3). This is why only $J_0$ appears in the radially symmetric vibrations of a drum, whose displacement is finite at the centre.

For $\nu = \frac12$ the roots $\pm\frac12$ differ by the integer 1, but here no logarithm appears: one finds the solutions $\frac{\sin x}{\sqrt x}$ and $\frac{\cos x}{\sqrt x}$, as the substitution $y = u/\sqrt x$, which turns the equation into $u'' + u = 0$, confirms. So in case 4 the constant $a$ can indeed be zero.

blocks.title: A series from a first-order equation
blocks.body: Let $f(x) = \dfrac{\arcsin x}{\sqrt{1 - x^2}}$ on $(-1, 1)$. Show that $(1 - x^2)f' - xf = 1$, and use this to find the Maclaurin series of $f$.
blocks.solution:
By the product rule, $f' = \frac{1}{1-x^2} + \frac{x\arcsin x}{(1-x^2)^{3/2}}$; multiplying by $1 - x^2$ gives $(1-x^2)f' = 1 + xf$, as claimed. The function $f$ is odd, and analytic on $(-1,1)$ as the product of two power series with radius 1. Write $f = \sum a_nx^n$ with $a_0 = 0$. Comparing coefficients of $x^n$ in $(1 - x^2)f' - xf = 1$:

$$n = 0: \ a_1 = 1, \qquad n \ge 1: \ (n+1)a_{n+1} - (n-1)a_{n-1} - a_{n-1} = 0,$$

so $a_{n+1} = \frac{n}{n+1}a_{n-1}$. Hence $a_3 = \frac23$, $a_5 = \frac45\cdot\frac23 = \frac{8}{15}$ and in general

$$\frac{\arcsin x}{\sqrt{1-x^2}} = \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{2\cdot4\cdots(2n)}{3\cdot5\cdots(2n+1)}x^{2n+1} = \sum_{n\ge0}\frac{4^n(n!)^2}{(2n+1)!}x^{2n+1}.$$

A direct attempt to multiply the series of $\arcsin x$ and $(1-x^2)^{-1/2}$ would be far messier.

blocks.body:
- Shift indices so every sum is in the same power $x^n$ before equating coefficients, and keep track of where each shifted sum starts: the leftover low-order terms (like $2a_2 = 0$ for Airy) are part of the recurrence.
- The guaranteed radius is the distance to the nearest complex singularity of $p$ and $q$, not the nearest real one.
- Write the equation with leading coefficient 1 before deciding whether a point is ordinary, regular singular or irregular. At an irregular singular point (for example $x^3y'' + y = 0$ at $0$) the Frobenius ansatz generally fails.
- In the Frobenius case, the smaller indicial root may fail to give a solution when the roots differ by an integer; the larger root always works.
- The series is a solution only inside its interval of convergence; a partial sum is an approximation, not a solution.

The functions produced here are among the special functions of analysis: the Bessel functions $J_
u(x) = \sum_k rac{(-1)^k}{k!\,\Gamma(k+
u+1)}(x/2)^{2k+
u}$ involve the [[gamma|gamma function]], and Legendre and Bessel functions are eigenfunctions of singular [[sturm-liouville]] problems. They arise when the [[heat-equation]], [[wave-equation]] or [[laplace-equation]] is separated in polar or spherical coordinates. In the complex plane, the Frobenius method is the beginning of the theory of linear equations with regular singular points, which leads to hypergeometric functions and monodromy, and it relies on the theory of [[holomorphic]] functions and [[continuation|analytic continuation]]. The same 'substitute a series' idea also gives Taylor-series methods in [[numerical-odes]].
